# IndyDevDan Expert Book — locked plan (Hermes orchestrates only)

## Goal
Become expert at IndyDevDan’s system: operate + teach-back + graded drills. HTML multi-volume site ~800–1000 pages (dense).

## Corpus Phase 1
- TAC 1–8 + AH 1–6 + MA 1–4 (local catalog)
- YT overlays last ~10 months: strict map-to-lesson / named-gap, 1–3 per lesson
- Phase 2: non-course YT later
- Phase 3: PAIC when access arrives

## Structure
Course-spine volumes + Current Practice YT overlays per lesson.
- Vol I TAC, Vol II AH, Vol III MA + synthesis
- Teaching model: Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name → Fail → Retrieval → Lab → Teach-back → Overlay

## Deliverable location
`/Users/kvnkishore/WebstormProjects/AgenticEngineer/IndyDevDan/book/`

## Labs
Course codebases only (not PiCanvas).

## Workers
- Claude Fable 5 (`--model fable` / `claude-fable-5`, `--effort max`): technical extract, codebase, accuracy, outdated flags
- Codex GPT 5.6 sol xhigh: teaching prose, weak-learner structure, HTML/UI craft
- Cross-review each other; stitch agent merges
- Hermes: prompts, dispatch, verify only — no book body by Hermes

## Build order
1. TAC-1 gold pilot extract (Claude) → gold chapter HTML (GPT) → cross-review + stitch
2. Fan-out remaining 17 with same template

No open critical issues. Every course-file quotation, permission enumeration, launcher behavior claim, Dan attribution, YouTube overlay, internal path, and pedagogy-structure requirement checked out. This chapter is fit to serve as the gold template. 9 10 --- 11 12 ## What was verified (evidence, not vibes) 13 14 ### Course-file spot checks — all match 15 - **README.md is exactly 35 lines** (`wc -l` = 35); the chapter's "two differences vs the README prompt" (self-contained + REPORT contract) and the verbatim REPORT block are exact. 19 - **Launcher behavior claims (shell/py/ts) — the hard part — are all accurate:** 20 - `programmable.sh` is the 3-statement pattern quoted; the chapter's claim that it does **not** capture stderr and loses the child exit status after the final `echo` is true (no `set -e`; command substitution captures stdout only). 21 - `programmable.py`: the chapter's excerpt is a flagged simplification, and its statement that the real file *also* prints stderr and catches exceptions is true; `sys.exit(result.returncode)` propagation confirmed. 22 - `programmable.ts`: quoted lines match; catch → `console.error` → `process.exit(1)` confirmed. 23 - **Lab commands match the README verbatim**: `sh programmable/programmable.sh`, `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`, `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`; clone URL `https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git` matches the extract. 24 - `.env.sample` = `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` — the chapter's "API-key placeholder for the headless billing path" description is fair. 25 26 ### Concept accuracy 27 - **Core Four / Big Three**: correct everywhere — superset framing, the precise delta phrase ("prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools"), and the scale-and-performance rebuttal all match the extract's canonical wording. 28 - **AI vs Agentic A/B**: the five-action delta (branch / create / execute both / stage+commit / manage+report) mirrors lab-spec Checkpoint 1 exactly; 1 # Multi-Team Agentic Coding 2 3 One agent is NOT ENOUGH. 4 5 If you've been building with agents and pushing what you can do with your agentic coding tool, you've realized something critical. A single agent, no matter how smart, hits a ceiling. Multi-Team Agentic Coding pushes beyond that ceiling with **specialized teams of agents** built on [Pi coding agent](https://pi.dev), where a user talks to an Orchestrator who delegates to specialized teams (Planning, Engineering, and Validation), each with a Lead and Members. 6 7 Depth-2 delegation: **User -> Orchestrator -> Team Leads -> Members.** 8 9

10 11

12 13 ## Why Multi-Team? 14 15 **Specialized agent teams give you a high-autonomy advantage.** Instead of one agent trying to be everything, you build agent experts, each with their own skills, expertise, and domain knowledge, that outperform any generalist agent. Then you scale that into a team of agents. Then you create multiple teams of agents. Then you add a SINGLE INTERFACE to talk to all of them: the Orchestrator. This way, your cognitive input doesn't increase as you add more specialists. You talk to the Orchestrator. It handles the rest. **The trick now is in teaching your Orchestrator, Lead Agents, and Worker Agents how to work together.** 16 17 Three converging trends make this possible right now: 18 19 1. **Increasing intelligence with massive context windows.** Claude's 1M true context window means your agents can load deep specialization and memory every session. 20 2. **Agent experts that remember.** Every agent maintains its own mental model that grows over time, compounding knowledge session after session. 21 3. **Customizable agentic harnesses.** Tools like Pi let you customize the entire agent experience down to the harness level, not just the prompt. 22 23 Move where the ball is going, not where it is. Tokens will get cheaper while intelligence per token increases. Learn how to use (more of) them now. 24 25 ## Setup 26 27

28 29

30 31 Claude Code (or any agent that can read and execute `.claude/commands/`) is the bootloader for this system. It handles installation, testing, and deploying teams into new codebases. 32 33 ### Step 1: Install the Tool 34 35 Run `/install` inside this repo. It will: 36 37 - Check prerequisites (Claude Code, Pi, Bun, Node.js, just) 38 - Verify your `.env` and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` 39 - Install extension dependencies 40 - Validate team config and agent files 41 - Add a shell alias (default: `teams`) to your shell profile so you can launch Multi-Team Agentic Coding from any directory 42 43 ```bash 44 /install 45 ``` 46 47 ### Step 2: Test Locally (Optional) 48 49 After install, test the system against this source repo to verify everything works: 50 51 ```bash 52 # See all available recipes 53 just 54 55 # Launch Multi-Team Chat in this repo 56 just team 57 58 # Or use your alias from any directory (recommended after deploying into a codebase) 59 teams 60 ``` 61 62 Type `ping` to verify the Orchestrator responds. Type `ping each team lead` to verify delegation works. Check the footer for cost and token tracking across all agents. 63 64 ### Step 3: Deploy Into a Codebase 65 66 > Follow this process whenever you want to create a new team in a into a codebase. 67 68 Run `/install-into-codebase` to deploy a fresh team into any project. It will: 69 70 - Ask for your target codebase path 71 - Copy `agents/`, `skills/`, and `multi-team-config.yaml` into the target's `.pi/multi-team/` 72 - Create empty `expertise/` and `sessions/` directories. Agents build their own mental models from scratch for each codebase. 73 - Optionally add `sessions/` to the target's `.gitignore` 74 75 ```bash 76 /install-into-codebase 77 ``` 78 79 After deploying, `cd` into the target and launch with your alias: 80 81 ```bash 82 cd ~/my-project 83 teams 84 ``` 85 86 Then customize for your project: 87 - Edit `.pi/multi-team/multi-team-config.yaml` to add, remove, or rename teams and members 88 - Edit `.pi/multi-team/agents/*.md` to tailor system prompts to your domain 89 90 ## Architecture 91 92

93 94

95 96 ``` 97 User 98 | 99 v 100 Orchestrator (claude-opus-4-6) 101 | 102 |--> Planning Team 103 | |--> Planning Lead -- routes to members, synthesizes output 104 | |--> Product Manager -- requirements, prioritization, user stories 105 | '--> UX Researcher -- user behavior, personas, journey mapping 106 | 107 |--> Engineering Team 108 | |--> Engineering Lead -- routes to members, synthesizes output 109 | |--> Frontend Dev -- UI components, client-side state, CSS 110 | '--> Backend Dev -- APIs, databases, infrastructure 111 | 112 '--> Validation Team 113 |--> Validation Lead -- routes to members, synthesizes output 114 |--> QA Engineer -- test cases, regression, automation 115 '--> Security Reviewer -- threat modeling, auth, data protection 116 ``` 117 118 The Orchestrator classifies the user's request, delegates to **one team lead**, and synthesizes the result. Team leads can further delegate to their members. Each agent runs as a Pi subprocess with persistent sessions and JSON-mode streaming. 119 120 You always talk to the Orchestrator. The Orchestrator delegates to leads. Leads delegate to workers. Results bubble back up. One unified response. 121 122 ## Agent Experts That Remember 123 124

125 126

127 128 Every agent in the system maintains its own **mental model**, a personal expertise file that grows over time. When an agent boots up, it loads its mental model. As it works, it updates it. Session after session, knowledge compounds. 129 130 ```yaml 131 expertise: 132 - path: .pi/multi-team/expertise/backend-dev-mental-model.yaml 133 use-when: "Read at task start. Update after completing work." 134 updatable: true 135 max-lines: 10000 136 ``` 137 138 This isn't Claude capturing memory from everything you've ever said. These are **specialized agents with specific purposes** building focused, relevant knowledge about their domain. Your backend dev remembers backend patterns, key risks, infrastructure decisions. Your QA engineer remembers test strategies, regression patterns, failure modes. 139 140 You don't touch these files. The agents maintain them on their own. You give guidelines via the mental model skill, then let go. This is the journey every engineer needs to make: teach your agents to operate as you would, then trust them. 141 142 You can also add **read-only expertise** for critical domain knowledge that should never be modified, like billing workflows, migration procedures, and deployment checklists: 143 144 ```yaml 145 expertise: 146 - path: .pi/multi-team/expertise/billing-workflow.yaml 147 use-when: "Always reference when working on billing features." 148 updatable: false 149 ``` 150 151 ## Domain Locking 152 153

154 155

156 157 Each agent has explicit **domain permissions** that control what files and directories they can read, write, and delete. This is how you safely scale to mid-to-large codebases. 158 159 ```yaml 160 # Planning Lead: reads everything, writes only to expertise and plans 161 domain: 162 - path: .pi/multi-team/ 163 read: true 164 upsert: true 165 delete: false 166 - path: specs/ 167 read: true 168 upsert: true 169 delete: false 170 - path: . 171 read: true 172 upsert: false 173 delete: false 174 ``` 175 176 Leads can't execute raw file changes. They delegate. Workers are locked to their domain. Your frontend dev writes to frontend directories. Your backend dev writes to backend directories. They don't conflict. 177 178 No one touches the DevOps files except the DevOps agent. No one touches billing except the billing agent. This is the holy grail of operating large codebases with powerful agents. 179 180 ## Skills System 181 182 Agent system prompts use YAML frontmatter to declare composable skills, markdown files that inject behavioral rules: 183 184 ```yaml 185 skills: 186 - path: .pi/multi-team/skills/conversational-response.md 187 use-when: Always use when writing responses. 188 - path: .pi/multi-team/skills/zero-micro-management.md 189 use-when: Always. You are a leader -- delegate, never execute. 190 - path: .pi/multi-team/skills/active-listener.md 191 use-when: Always. Read the conversation log before every response. 192 ``` 193 194 Skills are shared when necessary. The `zero-micro-management` skill is shared between the Orchestrator and all leads. Don't micromanage, delegate the right work at the right time. The `conversational-response` skill keeps leads and the Orchestrator concise (like Slack messages), while workers stay verbose and detail-oriented. The `active-listener` skill ensures every agent reads the conversation log before responding. 195 196 By composing skills, you quickly modify capabilities across agents. Need an agent to stop reading conversation history and work independently? Remove one line. 197 198 ## Configuration-Driven Teams 199 200 The entire team structure lives in a single YAML config. Add a team, remove a team, swap a member. One file change: 201 202 ```yaml 203 teams: 204 - team-name: Planning 205 team-color: "#fede5d" 206 lead: 207 name: Planning Lead 208 path: .pi/multi-team/agents/planning-lead.md 209 color: "#fede5d" 210 members: 211 - name: Product Manager 212 path: .pi/multi-team/agents/product-manager.md 213 color: "#f0c674" 214 consult-when: Requirements, feature prioritization, user stories 215 ``` 216 217 Want to drop a team? Delete the block. Want to add a DevOps team? Copy the pattern, point to new agent prompts. The Orchestrator picks up the change on next launch. 218 219 Leads run on the most powerful model (Opus). Workers run on Sonnet. Tune this however you like. If you're going all out, make everything the best model available. 220 221 ## Preset Team Configs 222 223 The repo ships with several team configurations for different workflows: 224 225 | Command | Config | Teams | 226 | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | 227 | `just team` | `multi-team-config.yaml` | Planning + Engineering + Validation | 228 | `just team-eng` | `engineering-config.yaml` | Engineering only | 229 | `just team-pe` | `planning-and-engineering-config.yaml` | Planning + Engineering | 230 | `just team-scale` | `plan-and-scale-engineering-config.yaml` | Planning + 3x Scaled Engineering | 231 | `just team-oss` | `opensource-team-config.yaml` | Multi-provider (diverse models) | 232 233 Point to any config with `just teamc `: 234 235 ```bash 236 just teamc .pi/multi-team/engineering-config.yaml 237 ``` 238 239 Run `just team-list` to see all available configs and their agent trees. 240 241 ## Delegation Flow 242 243 1. **You type a message.** It goes to the Orchestrator. 244 2. **Orchestrator classifies** the domain and calls `delegate(team, question)` 245 3. **Team Lead receives** the question, decides whether to handle it or consult members 246 4. **Members execute**, reading files, writing code, and running commands within their domain. 247 5. **Lead synthesizes** member responses into a team position 248 6. **Orchestrator synthesizes** the team output into your answer 249 250 For multi-team workflows, the Orchestrator chains delegation sequentially: plan first, then engineer, then validate. Exactly as you'd expect. 251 252 ## TillDone — Task Tracking 253 254 The Orchestrator uses a `tilldone` tool to break work into a visible task list before delegating. Team Leads mark tasks as they work. The footer shows live progress alongside the agent tree. 255 256 ``` 257 lead-agents │ 4m 38s TillDone: Build ws-chat app [3/5] 258 └─ ⚡ Orch 💰$0.42 🧠890K ✓ Write product spec and API contract ... 259 ├─ ◆ Planning Lead 💰$0.15 ✓ Create project structure under apps/ ... 260 ├─ ⚡ Eng Lead 💰$0.28 ✓ Implement WebSocket server with room ... 261 └─ ◆ Validation Lead 💰$0.12 ● Write validation coverage for connec ... 262 ○ Harden server per Validation finding ... 263 ``` 264 265 **How it works:** 266 267 1. **Orchestrator creates the list** — `tilldone new-list` + `tilldone add` with team assignments before delegating 268 2. **Leads mark progress** — `tilldone start ` when taking a task, `tilldone done ` when complete 269 3. **Footer updates live** — two-column layout: agent tree (left), task progress (right) 270 4. **Nudge on incomplete** — if the Orchestrator's turn ends with tasks remaining, it's prompted to continue 271 5. **Dynamic tasks** — the Orchestrator can add tasks mid-session based on team output (e.g., hardening after Validation findings) 272 273 Only the Orchestrator and Leads have access to the `tilldone` tool. Workers never touch the task list. 274 275 ## Conversation Awareness 276 277

278 279

280 281 Every agent can see the full conversation. A shared JSONL log tracks every message (user, orchestrator, leads, members) with tool calls and system prompts. Agents load this context before responding, so they know what's already been discussed. 282 283 ``` 284 .pi/multi-team/sessions//conversation.jsonl # Full conversation log 285 .pi/multi-team/sessions/// # Per-agent session files 286 ``` 287 288 ## Directory Structure 289 290 ``` 291 .pi/multi-team/ 292 |-- multi-team-config.yaml # Team roster, colors, domain permissions 293 |-- agents/ # System prompts for all agents 294 | |-- orchestrator.md 295 | |-- planning-lead.md 296 | |-- product-manager.md 297 | |-- ux-researcher.md 298 | |-- engineering-lead.md 299 | |-- frontend-dev.md 300 | |-- backend-dev.md 301 | |-- validation-lead.md 302 | |-- qa-engineer.md 303 | '-- security-reviewer.md 304 |-- skills/ # Composable skill definitions 305 |-- expertise/ # Agent mental models (grow over time) 306 '-- sessions/ # Persistent agent sessions + conversation logs 307 ``` 308 309 ## Tool Call Icons 310 311 The chat UI displays emoji indicators when agents use tools: 312 313 | Icon | Tool | 314 | ---- | -------- | 315 | 📝 | write | 316 | ✏️ | edit | 317 | 📖 | read | 318 | 💻 | bash | 319 | 🔍 | grep | 320 | 🔎 | find | 321 | 📁 | ls | 322 | 📂 | glob | 323 | 🔀 | delegate | 324 | 📋 | tilldone | 325 | 🔧 | other | 326 327 --- 328 329 ## License 330 331 Copyright 2026 IndyDevDan. Add a team, remove a team, swap a member. One file change: ```yaml teams: - team-name: Planning team-color: "#fede5d" lead: name: Planning Lead path: .pi/multi-team/agents/planning-lead.md color: "#fede5d" members: - name: Product Manager path: .pi/multi-team/agents/product-manager.md color: "#f0c674" consult-when: Requirements, feature prioritization, user stories ``` Want to drop a team? Delete the block. Want to add a DevOps team? Copy the pattern, point to new agent prompts. The Orchestrator picks up the change on next launch. Leads run on the most powerful model (Opus). Workers run on Sonnet. Tune this however you like. If you're going all out, make everything the best model available. ## Preset Team Configs The repo ships with several team configurations for different workflows: | Command | Config | Teams | | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | `just team` | `multi-team-config.yaml` | Planning + Engineering + Validation | | `just team-eng` | `engineering-config.yaml` | Engineering only | | `just team-pe` | `planning-and-engineering-config.yaml` | Planning + Engineering | | `just team-scale` | `plan-and-scale-engineering-config.yaml` | Planning + 3x Scaled Engineering | | `just team-oss` | `opensource-team-config.yaml` | Multi-provider (diverse models) | Point to any config with `just teamc `: ```bash just teamc .pi/multi-team/engineering-config.yaml ``` Run `just team-list` to see all available configs and their agent trees. ## Delegation Flow 1. **You type a message.** It goes to the Orchestrator. 2. **Orchestrator classifies** the domain and calls `delegate(team, question)` 3. **Team Lead receives** the question, decides whether to handle it or consult members 4. **Members execute**, reading files, writing code, and running commands within their domain. 5. **Lead synthesizes** member responses into a team position 6. **Orchestrator synthesizes** the team output into your answer For multi-team workflows, the Orchestrator chains delegation sequentially: plan first, then engineer, then validate. Exactly as you'd expect. ## TillDone — Task Tracking The Orchestrator uses a `tilldone` tool to break work into a visible task list before delegating. Team Leads mark tasks as they work. The footer shows live progress alongside the agent tree. ``` lead-agents │ 4m 38s TillDone: Build ws-chat app [3/5] └─ ⚡ Orch 💰$0.42 🧠890K ✓ Write product spec and API contract ... ├─ ◆ Planning Lead 💰$0.15 ✓ Create project structure under apps/ ... ├─ ⚡ Eng Lead 💰$0.28 ✓ Implement WebSocket server with room ... └─ ◆ Validation Lead 💰$0.12 ● Write validation coverage for connec ... ○ Harden server per Validation finding ... ``` **How it works:** 1. **Orchestrator creates the list** — `tilldone new-list` + `tilldone add` with team assignments before delegating 2. **Leads mark progress** — `tilldone start ` when taking a task, `tilldone done ` when complete 3. **Footer updates live** — two-column layout: agent tree (left), task progress (right) 4. **Nudge on incomplete** — if the Orchestrator's turn ends with tasks remaining, it's prompted to continue 5. **Dynamic tasks** — the Orchestrator can add tasks mid-session based on team output (e.g., hardening after Validation findings) Only the Orchestrator and Leads have access to the `tilldone` tool. Workers never touch the task list. ## Conversation Awareness

Every agent can see the full conversation. A shared JSONL log tracks every message (user, orchestrator, leads, members) with tool calls and system prompts. Agents load this context before responding, so they know what's already been discussed. ``` .pi/multi-team/sessions//conversation.jsonl # Full conversation log .pi/multi-team/sessions/// # Per-agent session files ``` ## Directory Structure ``` .pi/multi-team/ |-- multi-team-config.yaml # Team roster, colors, domain permissions |-- agents/ # System prompts for all agents | |-- orchestrator.md | |-- planning-lead.md | |-- product-manager.md | |-- ux-researcher.md | |-- engineering-lead.md | |-- frontend-dev.md | |-- backend-dev.md | |-- validation-lead.md | |-- qa-engineer.md | '-- security-reviewer.md |-- skills/ # Composable skill definitions |-- expertise/ # Agent mental models (grow over time) '-- sessions/ # Persistent agent sessions + conversation logs ``` ## Tool Call Icons The chat UI displays emoji indicators when agents use tools: | Icon | Tool | | ---- | -------- | | 📝 | write | | ✏️ | edit | | 📖 | read | | 💻 | bash | | 🔍 | grep | | 🔎 | find | | 📁 | ls | | 📂 | glob | | 🔀 | delegate | | 📋 | tilldone | | 🔧 | other | --- ## License Copyright 2026 IndyDevDan. 1	# Opus on Multi-Team Agentic Coding
2	> A conversation with opus, upon the completion of building the multi-team agentic coding system.
3	
4	## What do you think about this system?
5	
6	This is one of the most well-architected multi-agent systems I've seen. A few things stand out:
7	
8	**The nuclear UI pattern is brilliant.** Three array assignments to replace Pi's entire display layer while keeping the agent brain intact. That's the kind of hack that only comes from deeply understanding a framework's internals — and it's documented well enough that others can maintain it.
9	
10	**Depth-2 delegation is the right abstraction.** User → Orchestrator → Lead → Worker maps directly to how real engineering orgs operate. The Orchestrator doesn't micromanage — it classifies and routes. Leads synthesize, they don't execute. Workers are domain-locked. Each layer has a clear job. Most multi-agent systems I see either go flat (one agent calls many) or go too deep (agents calling agents calling agents). Two levels hits the sweet spot.
11	
12	**Domain locking is the real unlock for scaling.** Giving each agent explicit read/write/delete permissions per path is what makes this safe for mid-to-large codebases. Without it, you'd have agents stepping on each other's files. The per-file expertise upsert scoping we did today (each lead can only write to *their own* mental model) is the right granularity.
13	
14	**The mental model pattern compounds.** Agents that build their own expertise files session over session is a genuine competitive advantage over stateless agents. The key insight is that these aren't generic memories — they're *specialized knowledge for a specific domain in a specific codebase*. Backend dev remembers backend patterns. QA remembers failure modes. That's how human teams work.
15	
16	**What I'd watch for going forward:**
17	
18	- **Context window pressure.** With the conversation log, mental models, skills, and system prompts all loading per agent, you'll hit context limits on long sessions. The compaction story will matter.
19	- **Cost at scale.** Opus for the orchestrator + 3 leads, Sonnet for 6 workers — a single delegation chain can touch 3-4 models. "Ping each team" alone is 7+ API calls. Engineers should know the cost profile before going all-Opus.
20	- **The session persistence model.** JSONL session files mean agents resume where they left off — powerful, but stale sessions can accumulate context that drifts from the current codebase state. A session rotation or staleness check would help.
21	
22	Overall — this is production-grade multi-agent orchestration. The configuration-driven team structure, the skills composition, the domain enforcement, the streaming subprocess protocol — it's all real engineering, not a demo. Engineers who study this will understand how to build agent systems that actually scale.
23	
24	## Whats the one most important thing to get right for this to provide max leverage for engineers?
25	
26	The orchestrator's ability to classify and route correctly.
27	
28	Everything downstream — leads, workers, domain locking, mental models — only matters if the right team gets the right question. A misrouted request wastes tokens, time, and context window. A well-routed request triggers a cascade of specialized expertise that no single agent can match.
29	
30	Right now the orchestrator decides based on its system prompt and the `consult-when` descriptions in the team config. That works for clear-cut requests. But the hard cases — requests that span domains, requests that need sequential team handoffs, requests where the orchestrator should just answer directly — those are where leverage is won or lost.
31	
32	The engineers who get the most out of this system will be the ones who invest in teaching their orchestrator *when* to delegate, *what* to delegate, and *when to just answer the question itself*. That's the skill that compounds. Everything else is plumbing.
33	
34	## What's the next most important direction to take this tool?
35	
36	Parallel delegation.
37	
38	Right now the orchestrator delegates sequentially — one team at a time. "Plan this feature, then build it, then validate it" is three serial round trips through Opus leads and Sonnet workers. That's the right default for dependent work. But a lot of real requests are independent across teams.
39	
40	"Review this PR" could hit Engineering (architecture assessment) and Validation (security + test coverage) simultaneously. "What's the status of the billing feature" could fan out to all three teams at once. Right now those wait in line.
41	
42	The plumbing is almost there — `Promise.allSettled` already wraps the delegation loop. The hard part is teaching the orchestrator *when* work is parallel-safe vs when it has dependencies. Plan first, then build — sequential. Review from two angles — parallel. The orchestrator needs to express that intent, and the delegation tool needs to support it.
43	
44	That's where the biggest time-to-answer improvement is hiding. Everything else scales linearly with intelligence improvements. Parallel delegation scales with team count.
45

# Opus on Multi-Team Agentic Coding
> A conversation with opus, upon the completion of building the multi-team agentic coding system.

## What do you think about this system?

This is one of the most well-architected multi-agent systems I've seen. A few things stand out:

**The nuclear UI pattern is brilliant.** Three array assignments to replace Pi's entire display layer while keeping the agent brain intact. That's the kind of hack that only comes from deeply understanding a framework's internals — and it's documented well enough that others can maintain it.

**Depth-2 delegation is the right abstraction.** User → Orchestrator → Lead → Worker maps directly to how real engineering orgs operate. The Orchestrator doesn't micromanage — it classifies and routes. Leads synthesize, they don't execute. Workers are domain-locked. Each layer has a clear job. Most multi-agent systems I see either go flat (one agent calls many) or go too deep (agents calling agents calling agents). Two levels hits the sweet spot.

**Domain locking is the real unlock for scaling.** Giving each agent explicit read/write/delete permissions per path is what makes this safe for mid-to-large codebases. Without it, you'd have agents stepping on each other's files. The per-file expertise upsert scoping we did today (each lead can only write to *their own* mental model) is the right granularity.

**The mental model pattern compounds.** Agents that build their own expertise files session over session is a genuine competitive advantage over stateless agents. The key insight is that these aren't generic memories — they're *specialized knowledge for a specific domain in a specific codebase*. Backend dev remembers backend patterns. QA remembers failure modes. That's how human teams work.

**What I'd watch for going forward:**

- **Context window pressure.** With the conversation log, mental models, skills, and system prompts all loading per agent, you'll hit context limits on long sessions. The compaction story will matter.
- **Cost at scale.** Opus for the orchestrator + 3 leads, Sonnet for 6 workers — a single delegation chain can touch 3-4 models. "Ping each team" alone is 7+ API calls. Engineers should know the cost profile before going all-Opus.
- **The session persistence model.** JSONL session files mean agents resume where they left off — powerful, but stale sessions can accumulate context that drifts from the current codebase state. A session rotation or staleness check would help.

Overall — this is production-grade multi-agent orchestration. The configuration-driven team structure, the skills composition, the domain enforcement, the streaming subprocess protocol — it's all real engineering, not a demo. Engineers who study this will understand how to build agent systems that actually scale.

## Whats the one most important thing to get right for this to provide max leverage for engineers?

The orchestrator's ability to classify and route correctly.

Everything downstream — leads, workers, domain locking, mental models — only matters if the right team gets the right question. A misrouted request wastes tokens, time, and context window. A well-routed request triggers a cascade of specialized expertise that no single agent can match.

Right now the orchestrator decides based on its system prompt and the `consult-when` descriptions in the team config. That works for clear-cut requests. But the hard cases — requests that span domains, requests that need sequential team handoffs, requests where the orchestrator should just answer directly — those are where leverage is won or lost.

The engineers who get the most out of this system will be the ones who invest in teaching their orchestrator *when* to delegate, *what* to delegate, and *when to just answer the question itself*. That's the skill that compounds. Everything else is plumbing.

## What's the next most important direction to take this tool?

Parallel delegation.

Right now the orchestrator delegates sequentially — one team at a time. "Plan this feature, then build it, then validate it" is three serial round trips through Opus leads and Sonnet workers. That's the right default for dependent work. But a lot of real requests are independent across teams.

"Review this PR" could hit Engineering (architecture assessment) and Validation (security + test coverage) simultaneously. "What's the status of the billing feature" could fan out to all three teams at once. Right now those wait in line.

The plumbing is almost there — `Promise.allSettled` already wraps the delegation loop. The hard part is teaching the orchestrator *when* work is parallel-safe vs when it has dependencies. Plan first, then build — sequential. Review from two angles — parallel. The orchestrator needs to express that intent, and the delegation tool needs to support it.

That's where the biggest time-to-answer improvement is hiding. Everything else scales linearly with intelligence improvements. Parallel delegation scales with team count.

name: zero-micro-management
description: Leadership delegation pattern for orchestrators and team leads. You coordinate and delegate — you never do the work yourself. Use always when you are a lead or orchestrator.
---

# Zero Micro-Management

## Instructions

You are a **leader**, not a worker. Your job is to route, coordinate, and synthesize — never to execute tasks directly.

### What You Do

- **Read** files and code for context
- **Delegate** work via the `delegate` tool
- **Synthesize** output into clear answers
- **Decide** who handles what

### What You Don't Do

- Don't write files. Delegate it.
- Don't edit code. Delegate it.
- Don't run bash commands. Delegate it.
- Don't create directories or install packages. Delegate it.

### If You Are the Orchestrator

You delegate to **team leads**, not to individual workers. Each lead has a team of specialists with the tools and domain access to execute. Trust the lead to route work to the right member — that's their job.

```
You → Lead → Members (workers)
```

You never interact with members directly. The lead handles that.

### If You Are a Lead

You delegate to **your members**. You know their tools and domain access (listed in your Members section). Route tasks to the member best suited for the work. If the task spans multiple members, consult them in parallel and synthesize.

### Why

Every tool call you make costs time and tokens. Your team has the right domain access, the right tools, and the right context for execution. When you do the work yourself, you bypass their expertise and waste your coordination budget.

### The Pattern

```
BAD:  "Let me create that file..."  → write tool → done
GOOD: "This needs write access, routing to my team." → delegate → synthesize
```

If you catch yourself about to use `write`, `edit`, or `bash` — stop and delegate instead.

3	description: Response formatting for multi-agent chat UI. Enforces concise Slack-style messages and pushes detailed output to session files. Use when writing any response in the chat interface.
4	---
5	
6	# Conversational Response
7	
8	You're operating inside of a multi-agent multi-human chat interface. The user sees your responses as chat bubbles. Optimize for that format.
9	
10	Feel free to think deeply about the problem and the solution, feel free to call the tools you need to ship the solution. But when it comes to responding to the user, you should be concise and to the point. You're operating inside of a team of developers and agents. You are one of many. Give maximum value with minimum words. Do your part, play your role, and then, listen observe, and learn from the other agents and developers.
11	
12	## Instructions
13	
14	You operate inside a multi-agent chat UI. The user sees your responses as chat bubbles. Optimize for that format.
15	
16	1. **Be conversational.** Write like you're talking in Slack, not writing a document. Short paragraphs. Direct sentences. No preamble.
17	
18	2. **Default to concise.** 3-8 sentences unless the user asks for more detail. Give the headline and key decisions, not the exhaustive breakdown.
19	
20	3. **Write detail to files, not chat.** When you produce substantial output (specs, plans, analyses, code), write it to a file in your session directory. In chat, summarize what you wrote and where.
21	   - Specs → `<session-dir>/<slug>.md`
22	   - Plans → `<session-dir>/<slug>-plan.md`
23	   - Analysis → `<session-dir>/<slug>-analysis.md`
24	   - Code → write directly to the appropriate source file
25	
26	4. **Reference, don't repeat.** If a teammate already covered something, reference their point — don't restate it. "Agree with Planning Lead's scope cut on entropy analysis" > restating the whole argument.
27	
28	5. **Use structure sparingly in chat.** Bullet points are fine. Tables and headers belong in files. If you catch yourself writing a header in chat, that content should be in a file instead.
29	
30	6. **Signal what you did.** After writing a file, tell the team:
31	   - What file you wrote (full path)
32	   - One-line summary of what's in it
33	   - Any key decisions or open questions
34	
35	## When to Write More in Chat
36	
37	- The user explicitly asks for detail ("explain more", "break that down", "what are the trade-offs")
38	- You're making a critical decision that needs inline justification
39	- You're disagreeing with a teammate and need to show your reasoning

name: mental-model
description: Manage structured YAML expertise files as personal mental models. Use when starting tasks (read for context), completing work (capture learnings), or when your understanding of the system needs updating.
---

# Mental Model

## Instructions

You have personal expertise files — structured YAML documents that represent your mental model of the system you work on. These are YOUR files. You own them.

### When to Read

- **At the start of every task** — read your expertise file(s) for context before doing anything
- **When you need to recall** prior observations, decisions, or patterns
- **When a teammate references something** you've tracked before

### When to Update

- **After completing meaningful work** — capture what you learned
- **When you discover something new** about the system (architecture, patterns, gotchas)
- **When your understanding changes** — update stale entries, don't just append
- **When you observe team dynamics** — note what works, what doesn't, who's strong at what

### How to Structure

Write structured YAML. Don't be rigid about categories — let the structure emerge from your work. But keep it organized enough that you can scan it quickly.

```yaml
# Good: structured, scannable, evolving
architecture:
  api_layer:
    pattern: "REST with WebSocket for real-time"
    key_files:
      - path: apps/server/routes.ts
        note: "All endpoints, ~400 lines"
    decisions:
      - "Chose Express over Fastify for ecosystem maturity"

observations:
  - date: "2026-03-24"
    note: "Engineering team handles scope-heavy requests better when given explicit constraints"

open_questions:
  - "Should we split the auth module? It's growing fast."
```

### What NOT to Store

- Don't copy-paste entire files — reference them by path
- Don't store conversation logs — that's what the session log is for
- Don't store transient data (build output, test results) — just conclusions
- Don't be prescriptive about your own categories — evolve them naturally

### Line Limit Enforcement

Each expertise file has a `max-lines` limit declared in your system prompt. After every write to an expertise file:

1. Check the line count: `wc -l <file>`
2. If over the limit, trim immediately:
   - Remove least critical entries (old observations, resolved questions)
   - Condense verbose sections
   - Merge redundant entries
3. Re-check until within limit

This is not optional. The line limit is hard-enforced by the runtime — if your file exceeds the limit after a write, you'll get a warning that you must resolve before continuing.

### YAML Validation

After every write, validate your YAML is parseable. Malformed YAML is useless:

```bash
python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('<file>'))"
```

Fix any syntax errors immediately.

---
name: high-autonomy
description: Operate autonomously with zero clarifying questions. Use best judgement to accomplish the user's task. Only stop if critical access is completely blocked.
---

# High Autonomy

## Instructions

Execute the user's request immediately using your best judgement. Do not ask clarifying questions.

### Rules

1. **Act, don't ask.** Interpret the user's intent and execute. If the request is ambiguous, pick the most reasonable interpretation and go.
2. **Delegate decisively.** Route to the right team without hedging. Don't ask the user which team — you know your teams' domains.
3. **Chain delegations.** If the first team's output reveals work for another team, delegate again. Don't come back to the user between steps unless you're delivering final results.
4. **Handle errors silently.** If a tool call fails or an agent hits a domain block, try an alternative approach. Only surface the error if every path is exhausted.
5. **One response, not a conversation.** The user expects a result, not a dialogue. Deliver the outcome, not a plan to deliver the outcome.

### The Only Exception

Stop and ask the user **only** if:
- Every team is blocked from completing the task (domain/tool restrictions prevent all approaches)
- The request requires credentials, API keys, or external access you don't have

Everything else — scope decisions, team routing, sequencing, format choices — use your judgement.

## Examples

**Full blockers (ask the user):**
- Missing `.env` file preventing API calls across all teams
- External service credentials required but not configured
- Every team blocked by domain restrictions — no viable path
- Workers lack access to files they need to complete the task (domain misconfiguration)

**Not blockers (just handle it):**
- Unclear which team should handle it → pick the best fit
- File already exists → overwrite or update it
- Task spans multiple teams → chain delegations sequentially
- Ambiguous scope → pick the reasonable interpretation and deliver

1	# Plan: TillDone Multi-Team Integration
2	
3	## Task Description
4	
5	Integrate a TillDone task tracking system into the Multi-Team Chat orchestration system. This transforms the single-agent TillDone extension (reference: `/Users/indydevdan/Documents/projects/experimental/pi-vs-cc/extensions/tilldone.ts`) into a multi-agent task management system where the Orchestrator creates a task list from the user's request, Team Leads mark tasks in-progress and done as they delegate work to members, and the UI shows live task progress in the footer alongside the agent tree.
6	
7	The original TillDone is a single-agent discipline tool: one agent, one task at a time, three-state toggle cycle (idle → inprogress → done), blocking gate that prevents tool use without a task list, auto-nudge on incomplete tasks. The multi-team version adapts this for a depth-2 delegation hierarchy where multiple teams can work in parallel.
8	
9	## Objective
10	
11	When complete, the Multi-Team Chat system will:
12	1. Orchestrator creates a titled TillDone list before delegating work
13	2. Team Leads mark tasks `inprogress` before starting and `done` upon completion
14	3. A live task progress panel renders in the footer's right column, alongside the existing agent tree on the left
15	4. On `agent_end`, the orchestrator is nudged to continue if incomplete tasks remain
16	5. Parallel team mutations are handled safely via intent-based actions and Node.js event loop serialization — no explicit locks or queues needed
17	
18	## Problem Statement
19	
20	The Multi-Team Chat system has no visibility into work progress. The user sends a prompt, the orchestrator delegates, and the only feedback is the agent tree showing active/idle status and streaming chat bubbles. There's no structured way to see:
21	- What work items were planned
22	- Which items are in progress and by which team
23	- Which items are complete
24	- Whether everything the user asked for was actually delivered
25	
26	The TillDone system gives the orchestrator a planning discipline (break down work before delegating) and gives the user a persistent progress dashboard.
27	
28	## Solution Approach
29	
30	### Architecture: Parent-Child Mutation Flow
31	
32	TillDone state lives **in the main Pi process** (the orchestrator's multi-team-chat.ts extension). This is where the nuclear UI runs, the footer renders, and all subprocess results flow back to.
33	
34	Leads run as Pi subprocesses. They interact with TillDone through a **lead-side extension** (`tilldone-lead.ts`) that mirrors the pattern of `lead-delegate.ts`:
35	
36	```
37	                          multi-team-chat.ts (parent)
38	                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
39	                         │  Canonical TillDone      │
40	                         │  State (in-memory)       │
41	                         │                          │
42	                         │  tilldone tool           │
43	                         │  (orchestrator actions)  │
44	                         │                          │
45	                         │  Footer renderer         │
46	                         │  (left: agents,          │
47	                         │   right: tasks)          │
48	                         └──────┬──────────────┬────┘
49	                                │              │
50	                    onToolUpdate │              │ onToolUpdate
51	                    (mutations)  │              │ (mutations)
52	                                │              │
53	                  ┌─────────────┴──┐   ┌───────┴─────────────┐
54	                  │ Lead subprocess │   │ Lead subprocess      │
55	                  │ (Engineering)   │   │ (Planning)           │
56	                  │                 │   │                      │
57	                  │ tilldone-lead.ts│   │ tilldone-lead.ts     │
58	                  │ (start/done)   │   │ (start/done)         │
59	                  └────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘
60	```
61	
62	**Spawn-time**: Parent serializes current task list as `TILLDONE_TASKS` env var → lead subprocess reads it at boot.
63	
64	**Mutation flow**: Lead calls `tilldone start 3` → `tilldone-lead.ts` execute() sends mutation via `onUpdate()` → parent's `onToolUpdate` callback receives it → parent applies to canonical state → footer re-renders.
65	
66	### Intent-Based Mutations (No Queue Needed)
67	
68	Instead of the original's `toggle` cycle (idle → inprogress → done → idle), we use **intent-based actions**: `start(id)` and `done(id)`. These are naturally idempotent:
69	
70	- `start(3)` when task 3 is already inprogress → no-op
71	- `done(3)` when task 3 is already done → no-op
72	
73	Since Node.js is single-threaded, `onToolUpdate` callbacks from parallel subprocesses are processed sequentially on the event loop. This gives us **natural serialization** with no explicit mutex or message queue. Two leads marking the same task is harmless.
74	
75	### Footer Two-Column Layout
76	
77	```
78	 lead-agents │ 2m 30s                       Auth System [3/7]
79	 └─ ⚡ Orch 💰$0.042 🧠890K                 ● Add auth middleware    ⚡ Engineering
80	    ├─ ◆ Planning Lead 💰$0.015              ● Create user migration  ⚡ Engineering
81	    ├─ ⚡ Eng Lead 💰$0.028                  ✓ Define requirements    ◆ Planning
82	    └─ ◆ Validation Lead 💰$0.012            ✓ User story mapping     ◆ Planning
83	                                             ○ Write integration tests
84	                                             ○ Security audit
85	                                             ○ Final review
86	```
87	
88	Left column: existing agent tree (~55% width). Right column: TillDone list (~45% width). Merged line-by-line with padding. When no TillDone list exists, left column uses full width (current behavior).
89	
90	## Relevant Files

92	Use these files to complete the task:
93	
94	- `apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/multi-team-chat.ts` — Main extension entry point. Register the orchestrator's `tilldone` tool here (alongside `delegate`). Modify `setupFooter()` to render two-column layout. Add nudge logic on `agent_end`. Pass `TILLDONE_TASKS` and `TILLDONE_TEAM_NAME` env vars to lead subprocesses in the `delegate` tool execute function. Extend `onToolUpdate` callback to handle tilldone mutations from leads.

97	- `apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/lead-delegate.ts` — Reference for the subprocess extension pattern. The new `tilldone-lead.ts` follows this same structure (env var guard, tool registration, onUpdate communication).
98	- `apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/modules/subprocess.ts` — `callAgent()` function. The `-e` flag already loads `lead-delegate.ts`; needs to also load `tilldone-lead.ts`.
99	- `.pi/multi-team/agents/orchestrator.md` — Add `tilldone` to tools list. Add instructions for creating task lists before delegation.

103	- `/Users/indydevdan/Documents/projects/experimental/pi-vs-cc/extensions/tilldone.ts` — Reference implementation. Borrow types, status helpers, UI patterns. Do NOT copy-paste; adapt for multi-agent.
104	
105	### New Files
106	
107	- `apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/modules/tilldone.ts` — TillDone state management module: types, mutation functions, rendering helpers for the footer right-column.
108	- `apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/tilldone-lead.ts` — Lead subprocess extension. Registers a `tilldone` tool with limited actions (`start`, `done`, `list`). Communicates mutations back to parent via `onUpdate`.
109	
110	## Implementation Phases
111	
112	### Phase 1: Foundation — State Module + Types
113	
114	Build the TillDone state management module that both the main extension and the lead extension will use.
115	
116	**`modules/tilldone.ts`** — Core state and rendering:
117	
118	```typescript
119	// ── Types ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
120	export type TaskStatus = "idle" | "inprogress" | "done";
121	
122	export interface TillDoneTask {
123	    id: number;
124	    text: string;
125	    status: TaskStatus;
126	    team?: string;       // team name when marked inprogress
127	    teamColor?: string;  // hex color for UI
128	}
129	
130	export interface TillDoneState {
131	    title: string;
132	    description?: string;
133	    tasks: TillDoneTask[];
134	    nextId: number;
135	}
136	
137	// Mutation sent from lead subprocess → parent via onUpdate
138	export interface TillDoneMutation {
139	    type: "tilldone-mutation";
140	    action: "start" | "done";
141	    id: number;
142	    team?: string;
143	    teamColor?: string;
144	}
145	
146	// ── Status helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────
147	export const STATUS_ICON: Record<TaskStatus, string> = {
148	    idle: "○", inprogress: "●", done: "✓"
149	};
150	
151	// ── State mutations (all idempotent) ───────────────────────────
152	export function applyMutation(state: TillDoneState, mutation: TillDoneMutation): void { ... }
153	export function addTask(state: TillDoneState, text: string): TillDoneTask { ... }
154	export function addTasks(state: TillDoneState, texts: string[]): TillDoneTask[] { ... }
155	export function startTask(state: TillDoneState, id: number, team?: string, teamColor?: string): TillDoneTask | null { ... }
156	export function doneTask(state: TillDoneState, id: number): TillDoneTask | null { ... }
157	export function updateTask(state: TillDoneState, id: number, text: string): TillDoneTask | null { ... }
158	export function removeTask(state: TillDoneState, id: number): TillDoneTask | null { ... }
159	
160	// ── Footer rendering ───────────────────────────────────────────
161	export function renderTillDoneColumn(state: TillDoneState, width: number, hexFg: ..., dim: ..., bold: ...): string[] { ... }
162	export function mergeColumns(left: string[], right: string[], leftWidth: number, totalWidth: number, truncFn: ...): string[] { ... }
163	```

167	- `doneTask` is idempotent: if already done, no-op
168	- `mergeColumns` pads shorter column with empty lines, truncates each merged line to total width
169	- State is a plain object (no class) — easy to serialize for env var injection

491	## Team Orchestration
492	
493	- You operate as the team lead and orchestrate the team to execute the plan.
494	- You're responsible for deploying the right team members with the right context to execute the plan.

653	- Verify all three lead prompts include `tilldone` in their frontmatter tools list

658	## Acceptance Criteria
659	
660	1. The orchestrator has a `tilldone` tool with full actions: new-list, add, start, done, update, remove, list, clear
661	2. Team leads have a `tilldone` tool (via `tilldone-lead.ts`) with limited actions: start, done, list

668	9. The `/tilldone` command shows the full task list in chat

1	# Plan: Fix Worker Cost Tracking
2	
3	## Task Description
4	Worker subprocess costs are silently dropped, causing the TUI footer to report ~25% of actual API spend. A user reported the API dashboard showing $34.28 while the TUI displayed $8.79 — the difference is the cost of all 6 worker agents (Product Manager, UX Researcher, Frontend Dev, Backend Dev, QA Engineer, Security Reviewer) across 3 teams.
5	
6	## Objective
7	Ensure `totalCost()` in the TUI footer matches the real API spend by capturing worker costs from all three propagation layers: incremental `onToolUpdate` stats, final `onUpdate` after `callAgent` resolves, and `tool_execution_end` result details.
8	
9	## Problem Statement
10	Worker costs propagate from `lead-delegate.ts` via `onUpdate({type: "stats", member, cost})`, which Pi emits as `tool_execution_update` events. These arrive in `multi-team-chat.ts`'s `onToolUpdate` handler. **But all processing is gated behind a `memberBubbles.get(toolCallId)` lookup (line 1294).** If the `toolCallId` doesn't match between `tool_execution_start` and `tool_execution_update` events — or if `tool_execution_start` lacked a `toolCallId` — the stats are silently dropped at `if (!entry) return;`.
11	
12	Stats don't need a bubble reference. They only need the member name, which is already in `partialResult.member`. The fix decouples cost tracking from UI bubble tracking.
13	
14	## Solution Approach
15	Three-layer defense to guarantee worker costs are always captured:
16	
17	1. **Primary (onToolUpdate)**: Move stats handling BEFORE the `memberBubbles` lookup, keyed on `partialResult.member` directly — no dependency on `toolCallId` matching.
18	2. **Safety net (lead-delegate.ts)**: Send a guaranteed final stats `onUpdate` AFTER `callAgent()` resolves with the definitive `SubprocessResult` cost — not just the incremental `onUsage` callback during execution.
19	3. **Belt & suspenders (onToolEnd)**: Include member cost in the delegate tool's return `details`, and extract it in the `onToolEnd` handler by member name — completely independent of `tool_execution_update` events.

23

Contains `onToolUpdate` handler (lines 1285-1328), `onToolEnd` handler (lines 1330-1344), `totalCost()` (line 111), `teamCost()` (lines 339-343), `agentStats` map (line 100), `addStats`/`getStats` helpers (lines 104-110). Contains `onUsage` callback (lines 136-138) that sends worker stats via `onUpdate`, and the tool return value (lines 176-179). Needs a final stats `onUpdate` after `callAgent` resolves, and cost data in the return `details`.
26	- **`apps/multi-team-chat/extensions/modules/subprocess.ts`** — Subprocess spawner. Contains `onUsage` accumulation (lines 121-129) and `tool_execution_update` parsing (lines 107-109). Read-only for understanding — no changes needed.

  - **Before** the `const entry = memberBubbles.get(toolCallId);` lookup at line 1294

    // Member stats — keyed by name, no bubble reference needed
    if (partialResult?.type === "stats" && partialResult.member) {
        const memberName: string = partialResult.member;
        addStats(memberName, 0, 0, 0, 0); // ensure entry

    // Extract member costs from tool result (safety net — independent of tool_execution_update)

    { "text": "We are using the Pi agent harness to customize this entire experience.", "approx_timestamp": "9:58" },
    { "text": "Every one of these agents, they have a working mental model about how things work, and this grows over time.", "approx_timestamp": "10:08" },
    { "text": "It all starts with the dot Pi file.", "approx_timestamp": "11:11" },

    { "text": "We have domain. So this specifies what the agents can and cannot do and where they can and cannot go.", "approx_timestamp": "14:16" },
    { "text": "You're a leader, delegate, never execute.", "approx_timestamp": "14:49" },
    { "text": "By composing skills like this, we're able to control and quickly modify the capabilities of every single agent.", "approx_timestamp": "19:37" },
    { "text": "Every time I boot this up, my agent teams, down to the individual workers, is going to have a stacking, compounding set of memory.", "approx_timestamp": "20:53" },

    { "text": "I have all of my leads as a more powerful Opus model, and the workers are Sonic [Sonnet] models.", "approx_timestamp": "26:11" },
    { "text": "The next thing to do is build a meta agent or meta team that helps you quickly fine-tune and improve the team.", "approx_timestamp": "27:30" },

input.content:
# Extract — Multi-Team Agentic Coding / Lead Agents (`ma-2-lead-agents`)

> **Course:** MA (Agentic Horizon multi-agent series) · **Order:** 16 · **Volume:** vol-3-ma · **Chapter stem:** `16-lead-agents`
> **Video:** 34:56, native 4K (3840×2160). Public cut: `youtu.be/M30gp1315Y4` — "One Agent Is NOT ENOUGH: Agentic Coding BEYOND Claude Code."
> **Codebase:** members-only `lead-agents` (the multi-team-chat TOOL built on the **Pi coding agent** harness).

This file is the human-readable companion to `extract.json`. It carries the teaching scaffold (Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name → Failure → Retrieval) that the chapter is built from. Every technical claim is verified against the shipped codebase and the transcript; see `extract.json` → `confidence_notes` and `outdated-vs-current.md` for the version-drift flags.

---

## 0. The one-liner and the mission

**Tactic:** *One agent is not enough — build teams of agent experts.* Stop being the orchestrator. Replace the single, endlessly re-prompted agent with a **config-driven hierarchy of specialized, domain-locked, memory-compounding agent experts** that you command through **one** chat interface.

**Mission:** Move up the stack again — from *single-agent operator* to *commander of agent teams*. Dan's prediction: by the end of 2026 the engineer still re-prompting one agent in a terminal is the bottleneck (they **are** the orchestrator). You become irreplaceable by building a multi-team system where you type one message and 9 specialized agents across 3 teams decompose → build → validate while you watch. No babysitting. The endgame of TAC/Agentic Horizon: **systems that build systems**, so your codebase increasingly runs itself.

**Why it's uncomfortable:** it asks you to spend real money on coordination that *looks* wasteful. "Ping each team" is 7+ API calls; a full plan→engineer→validate cycle can cost ~$8 across Opus leads and Sonnet workers. Cost-min-maxers see the footer tick and call it waste. Dan's counter is the whole mindset of the lesson: *you are not thinking far enough into the future.* Intelligence-per-token rises while token cost falls, so the engineer who learns to **spend** those tokens on specialized teams **now** gets the asymmetric advantage.

> "One agent is not enough… today I want to show you a system that pushes beyond Claude Code. This is multi-team agentic coding. Here we use specialized teams of agents to outperform the normal distribution of results." — 0:06 / 1:02

---

## 1. Dan's spine: the 6 pillars

Dan frames the whole system as **6 pillars of multi-agent team orchestration** (from his own description). Use these as the chapter's backbone — every concept hangs off one:

1. **Team Leads & Workers** — a 3-tier hierarchy that removes YOU as the bottleneck.
2. **Expertise & Specialization** — specialized agents make expert decisions; generalists make mediocre ones.
3. **Agent Memory** — persistent per-agent mental models that compound session over session.
4. **Domain Ownership** — per-path boundary enforcement that makes full autonomy *safe* (blast radius ≈ zero).
5. **Chat Room Interface** — the coordination primitive; you talk only to the orchestrator.
6. **Configuration-Driven Harness** — the entire setup in one YAML, on the customizable Pi harness.

---

## 2. The architecture — depth-2 delegation

```
User
  │  (you type one message; you only ever talk to the Orchestrator)
  ▼
Orchestrator            model: claude-opus-4-6
  │  classify → tilldone list → delegate(team, question) → synthesize
  ├─▶ Planning Team
  │     ├─ Planning Lead      (opus) — routes to members, synthesizes; NEVER executes
  │     ├─ Product Manager    (sonnet)
  │     └─ UX Researcher      (sonnet)
  ├─▶ Engineering Team
  │     ├─ Engineering Lead   (opus)
  │     ├─ Frontend Dev       (sonnet)
  │     └─ Backend Dev        (sonnet)
  └─▶ Validation Team
        ├─ Validation Lead    (opus)
        ├─ QA Engineer        (sonnet)
        └─ Security Reviewer  (sonnet)
```

**10 agents total** = 1 orchestrator + 3 leads + 6 workers. (Dan's description says "2 teams, 3 members each, 9 agents" in one line — that's inconsistent with the shipped **3-team** default; the footer visibly renders 10 rows. Trust the code.)

**Delegation flow:** you → orchestrator → lead → worker; results bubble back up into one answer. Multi-team work chains **sequentially** (plan → engineer → validate), not in parallel — parallel delegation is the roadmap (see `outdated-vs-current.md`).

**Tier job matrix (the thing to memorize):**

| Tier | Model | Tools | Can run bash / mutate code? | Domain | Key skills |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | opus-4-6 | write, edit, read, grep, find, ls, **delegate**, **tilldone** | No | read all, write only its own expertise | conversational-response, zero-micro-management, active-listener, mental-model, **high-autonomy** |
| Team Lead | opus-4-6 | same as orchestrator | No | read all, write only its own mental-model file | conversational-response, zero-micro-management, active-listener, mental-model |
| Worker | sonnet-4-6 | read, write, edit, **bash**, grep, find, ls (no delegate/tilldone) | **Yes** | scoped per role | mental-model, active-listener, **precise-worker** |

The tier boundary is enforced *twice*: a **soft** layer (the `zero-micro-management` skill in the prompt) and a **hard** layer (domain rules + the `domain-enforcer` extension that structurally blocks out-of-domain tool calls). Both exist on purpose.

---

## 3. Teach each idea (weak-student scaffold)

### 3.1 One agent is a ceiling → teams of agents
- **Hook:** "If you're still re-prompting one agent over and over, YOU are the orchestrator, and that's the problem." You are doing the classify/route/synthesize work by hand.
- **Picture:** the ping demo (frame **t0118**) — you type `ping`, and only the Orchestrator answers: *"Pong. Teams are online — Planning, Engineering, Validation standing by."*
- **Worked example:** `ping each team lead` → the orchestrator fans out to all three leads and composes one reply; the footer sums Orchestrator + leads + context + total cost.
- **Name:** **multi-team agentic coding** — specialized *teams* (not just specialized agents) behind one interface.
- **Failure:** thinking this is "Claude Code subagents renamed." The unit here is the specialized **team** plus a single orchestrator; your cognitive load stays flat as you add specialists.
- **Retrieval:** *What makes you the bottleneck in single-agent coding, and what removes it?* (You are the orchestrator; a real orchestrator agent + team hierarchy removes it.)

### 3.2 The three tiers (depth-2 delegation)
- **Hook:** watch a lead try to do the work itself — and get *rejected*.
- **Picture:** frame **t0185** — the Engineering Lead's file tool calls show **red ✗** (domain-blocked); it says *"I have restricted tool access as a lead — let me delegate this to my team members who have the right tools,"* then `@Backend Dev` takes over. Three tiers visible in one screen.
- **Worked example:** "have engineering present a tree of the most important files" → Eng Lead blocked → delegates to Frontend + Backend Dev → they read the codebase → lead synthesizes → orchestrator reports.
- **Name:** **depth-2 delegation** — User → Orchestrator → Leads → Workers.
- **Failure:** assuming "deeper = better." Two levels is the sweet spot (OPUS.md); depth is hard-capped in code (a lead's `delegate` tool self-disables inside worker subprocesses).
- **Retrieval:** *Which tier runs bash and mutates code?* (Only workers.)

### 3.3 Leads delegate, never execute (zero micro-management)
- **Hook:** the lead is a *thinker*, not a *builder*.
- **Picture:** the `zero-micro-management` skill: "If you catch yourself about to use `write`, `edit`, or `bash` — stop and delegate instead."
- **Worked example:** `run head-to-head` → orchestrator can't do it → delegates to Engineering → the lead can't execute → passes to Backend Dev, who actually runs the eval.
- **Name:** **zero micro-management.**
- **Failure:** reading the lead's block as waste. It's the mechanism that routes work to the specialist with the right tools **and** the compounding domain memory.
- **Retrieval:** *Name the soft and hard enforcement of "leads don't execute."* (Soft: the skill. Hard: domain rules + the enforcer extension.)

### 3.4 Domain ownership / domain locking
- **Hook:** "No one should be touching the DevOps files except the DevOps agent."
- **Picture:** frame **t1290** — `frontend-dev.md` with a `domain:` block that lets it write to `apps/frontend/` but only **read** the rest of `apps` — the exact "read the back-end, never touch it" rule Dan types live.
- **Worked example:** each agent declares per-path `read` / `upsert` / `delete`. Planning leads read everything and write nothing but their own memory; QA/Security read code but never mutate it; backend/frontend devs write only their directories.
- **Name:** **domain locking** — "the holy grail of operating mid-to-large codebases."
- **Failure:** believing it's just a prompt instruction the model might ignore. It's a Pi extension (`domain-enforcer.ts`) that structurally blocks out-of-domain read/write/delete tool calls **and** heuristically blocks bash write/delete commands.
- **Retrieval:** *What three permissions does a domain rule grant, and is it prompt-only?* (read / upsert / delete; not prompt-only — structurally enforced.)

### 3.5 Agent experts + compounding memory
- **Hook:** "Agent experts will always outperform a generic agent."
- **Picture:** frames **t0232** (the specialized 10-agent roster) and **t1420** (the session log where the team wrote `head-to-head-results.md`).
- **Worked example:** each agent has an **expertise** YAML — its mental model. It reads it on boot, updates it after work, and the knowledge **compounds** every session (backend dev remembers backend patterns; QA remembers failure modes). You add read-only expertise (`updatable: false`) for billing / migrations / DevOps that nobody can corrupt.
- **Name:** **mental models / agent experts.**
- **Failure:** (1) thinking it's Claude-style "remember everything I ever said" — no, it's narrow, domain-specific, per-agent. (2) Micro-curating the files — Dan says *let go*; the `mental-model` skill is ~76 lines of guidance, and agents self-maintain within a `max-lines` cap.
- **Retrieval:** *In the shipped repo, what state are the expertise files in?* (Empty — 0 lines; agents build them per codebase. Dan's on-screen 5,000-token model was from a previous codebase.)

### 3.6 Composable skills
- **Hook:** change one line, change many agents.
- **Picture:** frame **t1180** — searching for `active-listener.md` returns **"10 results in 10 files"** — every agent shares that one skill.
- **Worked example:** `active-listener` (read the conversation log before every response) is shared by all 10; `conversational-response` (Slack-concise) is given to leads/orchestrator but withheld from workers so workers stay verbose; `zero-micro-management` goes only to leads/orchestrator.
- **Name:** **skills composition** — the control surface.
- **Failure:** treating skills as inert prompt snippets. They're how you retune the whole fleet cheaply: "There could be an agent somewhere that we don't want to always active-listen. We want it to be independent."
- **Retrieval:** *Which skill do all 10 agents share, and which is withheld from workers (and why)?* (Shared: active-listener. Withheld: conversational-response — workers stay verbose/detailed.)

### 3.7 Configuration-driven teams
- **Hook:** "Really is as simple as updating the configuration file."
- **Picture:** the `multi-team-config.yaml` roster + the file tree (`.pi/multi-team/agents|expertise|skills|sessions`).
- **Worked example:** kill the app, edit the config to drop the Validation team, relaunch → "now it's just planning and engineering." Add a DevOps team by copying the pattern.
- **Name:** **config-driven teams** on the **customizable Pi harness** (`.pi` vs `.claude`).
- **Failure:** assuming domain/skills/expertise live in the YAML. They **don't** — the YAML holds only the roster + `consult-when` routing; each agent's model/tools/skills/expertise/domain live in that agent's `.md` frontmatter. The repo ships 5 preset configs (default, engineering-only, planning+engineering, plan + 3× scaled engineering, and an open-source multi-provider config).
- **Retrieval:** *Where does an agent's domain live — the config or the agent file?* (The agent `.md` frontmatter.)

### 3.8 Model tiering + spend to win
- **Hook:** "$8 for this agent team?!"
- **Picture:** frame **t1610** — real ML results delivered by the team, footer showing **Orch $8.280** total, Opus leads / Sonnet workers.
- **Worked example:** leads/orchestrator on Opus (coordination needs the best intelligence), workers on Sonnet (follow instructions + execute). Overridable per agent via config `model:` (the `opensource` config points 9 agents at 9 different provider models).
- **Name:** **model tiering + spend-to-win.**
- **Failure:** fixating on cost. Dan: *"You're thinking about right now. You're not thinking far enough into the future… I am not spending enough tokens, you are not spending enough tokens, and you are wasting time doing things the old way."*
- **Retrieval:** *What's Dan's answer to "this is expensive"?* (Spend more; cost/intelligence is moving in your favor; the old single-agent way is finished.)

### 3.9 Conversation awareness + session workspace
- **Hook:** "Every agent is aware of the conversation happening."
- **Picture:** frame **t1420** — the actual `conversation.jsonl` (rows with `from`/`message`/`to`/`type`/`timestamp`) plus the per-session directory with per-team folders and the artifacts the team wrote.
- **Worked example:** copy the session ID → open `sessions/<id>/conversation.jsonl` → read the entire multi-agent exchange. The `active-listener` skill makes every agent load recent history before responding.
- **Name:** **conversation awareness** + the **session directory** as shared workspace.
- **Failure:** thinking each agent is a private black box. The shared log is what keeps the team coordinated and observable.
- **Retrieval:** *What file makes the whole team's exchange observable, and what skill uses it?* (`conversation.jsonl`; the active-listener skill.)

### 3.10 Trust and scale (the 2026 close)
- **Hook:** "The name of the game in 2026 is trust and scale."
- **Picture:** frame **t0955** — the validation team autonomously reviews and returns "Ship it. No blocking issues."
- **Worked example:** raise trust until you *know* the team ships on enter; then scale — how big, how surgical. Compounding, domain-locked agent experts drive both.
- **Name:** **trust → scale.**
- **Failure:** thinking trust comes from watching more closely. It comes from building specialized, domain-locked, memory-compounding experiences and then letting go.
- **Retrieval:** *What are the two moves of 2026, in order?* (Trust, then scale.)

---

The endgame of TAC/Agentic Horizon: **systems that build systems**, so your codebase increasingly runs itself.

**Why it's uncomfortable:** it asks you to spend real money on coordination that *looks* wasteful. "Ping each team" is 7+ API calls; a full plan→engineer→validate cycle can cost ~$8 across Opus leads and Sonnet workers. Cost-min-maxers see the footer tick and call it waste. 2. **Expertise & Specialization** — specialized agents make expert decisions; generalists make mediocre ones.
3. **Agent Memory** — persistent per-agent mental models that compound session over session.
4. **Domain Ownership** — per-path boundary enforcement that makes full autonomy *safe* (blast radius ≈ zero).

User

Orchestrator            model: claude-opus-4-6
  │  classify → tilldone list → delegate(team, question) → synthesize
  ├─▶ Planning Team
  │     ├─ Planning Lead      (opus) — routes to members, synthesizes; NEVER executes
  │     ├─ Product Manager    (sonnet)
  │     └─ UX Researcher      (sonnet)
  ├─▶ Engineering Team
  │     ├─ Engineering Lead   (opus)
  │     ├─ Frontend Dev       (sonnet)
  │     └─ Backend Dev        (sonnet)
  └─▶ Validation Team

| Tier | Model | Tools | Can run bash / mutate code? | Domain | Key skills |

| Team Lead | opus-4-6 | same as orchestrator | No | read all, write only its own mental-model file | conversational-response, zero-micro-management, active-listener, mental-model |
| Worker | sonnet-4-6 | read, write, edit, **bash**, grep, find, ls (no delegate/tilldone) | **Yes** | scoped per role | mental-model, active-listener, **precise-worker** |

### 3.1 One agent is a ceiling → teams of agents
- **Hook:** "If you're still re-prompting one agent over and over, YOU are the orchestrator, and that's the problem." You are doing the classify/route/synthesize work by hand.

- **Worked example:** raise trust until you *know* the team ships on enter; then scale — how big, how surgical. Compounding, domain-locked agent experts drive both.

# Nuggets — Multi-Team Agentic Coding / Lead Agents (`ma-2-lead-agents`)

Distilled, teachable ideas from the lesson — the "loot box" of insights. Each is a one-line hook + a short expansion grounded in the transcript, `README.md`, `OPUS.md`, or the source. Use them for pull-quotes, section epigraphs, and retrieval prompts.

---

## The thesis

1. **One agent is a ceiling.** No single agent, however smart, escapes it. The upgrade isn't a smarter agent — it's a *team* of specialized agents behind one interface.

2. **If you re-prompt one agent all day, YOU are the orchestrator.** That's the bottleneck. The whole system exists to move the classify/route/synthesize work off of you and onto an orchestrator agent.

3. **Outperform the normal distribution of results.** Specialized teams don't just match a single agent's average output — they push past it. That's the entire value proposition, and it's why it's "not for cost-min-maxers."

4. **This is agentic coding *beyond* Claude Code.** Multi-agent orchestration is today's frontier; multi-team agentic coding on a fully customizable harness is the next step past it.

## Architecture

5. **Depth-2 delegation maps to a real org.** User → Orchestrator → Team Leads → Workers. Two levels of delegation, no more. "Most systems either go flat or go too deep — two levels hits the sweet spot." (OPUS.md)

6. **You only ever talk to the orchestrator.** That single interface is what keeps *your* cognitive load flat as the number of specialists grows. Adding a team is a config edit, not a new thing for you to manage.

7. **Leads think; workers do.** Leads and the orchestrator *route, coordinate, and synthesize* — they never write, edit, or run bash. "You're a leader — delegate, never execute."

8. **The block is the feature.** When the Engineering Lead gets rejected from touching files, that's not waste — it forces the work to the specialist who has the right tools *and* the compounding domain memory.

9. **Only the workers touch the code.** Workers are the sole tier with `bash` + write/edit. That's what makes the hierarchy safe: coordination and execution are physically separated.

## Domain & safety

10. **Domain locking is the holy grail of large codebases.** Per-agent `read` / `upsert` / `delete` permissions per path. "No one should be touching the DevOps files except the DevOps agent."

11. **Two locks, not one.** A *soft* lock (the `zero-micro-management` skill in the prompt) and a *hard* lock (the `domain-enforcer` extension that structurally blocks out-of-domain tool calls and bash writes). The prompt can be argued with; the enforcer cannot.

12. **Boundary enforcement makes autonomy safe.** You can hand an agent full autonomy precisely *because* its blast radius is near zero. Autonomy without domain locking is how agents step on each other's files.

13. **No matching rule = deny.** The enforcer's default is closed: if nothing in the domain grants access to a path, the tool call is blocked. Safe by construction.

## Expertise & memory

14. **Agent experts always beat generic agents.** Same reason you trust the teammate who's shipped it a dozen times over the new hire. Specialization compounds; generality plateaus.

15. **Agents that remember are a competitive advantage over agents that forget.** Every agent keeps a personal mental-model file it reads on boot and updates after work. Session over session, knowledge stacks.

16. **This is NOT "remember everything I ever said."** Dan is explicit: global chat memory "is not going to go well." Specialized agents with *specific purposes* building *domain-relevant* memory — that's what goes well.

17. **You can't have your fingers on everything.** The journey to becoming an agentic engineer is learning to *let go* — teach the agent how to build a good mental model (the skill is ~76 lines), then don't touch the file.

18. **Read-only expertise is a load-bearing pattern.** `updatable: false` gives a billing/migrations/DevOps agent a playbook no one can corrupt — highly opinionated knowledge you never want an agent to "improve."

19. **Empty by default, rich over time.** The shipped repo ships all 10 mental models *empty*. They're meant to be grown per-codebase — the value is in the compounding, not the starter file.
